# Introduction {#sec-intro}

According to Gallup, 22 percent of American workers worried technology would make their job obsolete in 2023, up seven percentage points from 2021 [@Gallup2023]. Concerns about automation were already evident years earlier. In 2017, the Pew Research Center reported that Americans expected automation to displace workers, although only 30 percent considered it likely that their own job would be replaced within their lifetime [@Pew2017]. Findings from the Pew and Gallup surveys suggest that concerns about automation have persisted over time. Concern of this kind is a belief about the future, and it need not track the work a place actually contains. Across the counties analyzed here, which together hold about 84 percent of the United States population [@census_popest2023], routine work averaged 39 percent of task content in 2023, and the middle half of counties ranged from 35 to 43 percent. We therefore wanted to investigate whether local economic patterns were consistent with concerns about disruption from automation.

If automation is a source of labor market disruption, evaluating its local economic relevance requires an outcome that captures how households experience those changes. Because prices differ substantially across counties, differences in nominal income overstate differences in what residents can afford [@Moretti2013]. We therefore test purchasing power as the outcome of interest. This motivates the use of purchasing power as a complementary measure of local economic conditions.

Three studies established the framework we build on. @Autor2003 showed that computers substitute for routine tasks and complement non-routine ones, which makes it possible to identify occupations exposed to automation. Applying that idea to local labor markets, @AutorDorn2013 documented polarization in routine intensive areas, where employment grew at both the high and low ends of the wage distribution while middle wage employment declined. @AcemogluAutor2011 then generalized the argument into a model in which tasks are the unit of production and skill groups compete to supply them.

Nevertheless, none of this work speaks directly to purchasing power at the county level. These studies report outcomes in unadjusted wages and employment counts rather than in what those wages buy locally. They work at a broader labor market geography than the county. They also fit linear specifications, which leaves open whether purchasing power moves with task groups in fixed dollar steps or in proportion. None of the three is a flaw in the earlier studies, which were built for other questions.

This study examines whether a county's task groups are associated with its purchasing power, and whether any such association survives controls for poverty and unemployment. We build a county by year panel covering 2008 to 2023, excluding 2020, from datasets published by federal agencies. Each county year is described by four task groups, routine cognitive, routine manual, non-routine cognitive, and non-routine manual, following the task framework of @Autor2003 and the occupation taxonomy of @AutorDorn2013, shown in @fig-taskframework. The outcome is purchasing power, measured in dollars as county median household income divided by the local price level from the Bureau of Economic Analysis Regional Price Parities. The panel holds 848 counties and 11,983 county year observations. @sec-data describes the sources and how the panel was built.

```{python}
#| label: fig-taskframework
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "**The Four Task Groups.** Each occupation falls in one cell of the Autor (2003) task framework. Routine tasks follow explicit rules that a machine can be programmed to carry out; non-routine tasks require judgment, adaptability, or in person interaction. Cognitive tasks work primarily with information; manual tasks work with physical objects and people. Occupation groupings follow Autor and Dorn (2013). Non-routine cognitive, outlined with a dashed border, is the reference group omitted from the regression."
%%R -w 8.5 -h 6 -u in -r 150 -b transparent
quad_df <- data.frame(
  group = c("Non-Routine Cognitive", "Non-Routine Manual", "Routine Cognitive", "Routine Manual"),
  col = c(2, 2, 1, 1),
  row = c(2, 1, 2, 1),
  examples = c("Management, engineering,\nteaching", "Food service, care work,\ncleaning",
               "Clerical, sales,\nclaims processing", "Production, assembly,\nmachine operation"),
  is_reference = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
)
quad_df$group_label <- gsub(" ", "\n", quad_df$group)
quad_df$linetype <- ifelse(quad_df$is_reference, "dashed", "solid")
quad_df$linewidth <- ifelse(quad_df$is_reference, 1.3, 0.9)

box_w <- 0.42; box_h <- 0.42

col_headers <- data.frame(
  col = c(1, 2),
  label = c("Routine", "Non-Routine")
)
row_headers <- data.frame(
  row = c(2, 1),
  label = c("Cognitive", "Manual")
)

ggplot(quad_df) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin=col-box_w, xmax=col+box_w, ymin=row-box_h, ymax=row+box_h,
                color=group, linetype=linetype, linewidth=linewidth),
            fill="#FCFCFB") +
  geom_text(aes(x=col, y=row+0.14, label=group_label, color=group),
            fontface="bold", size=4.6, lineheight=0.95) +
  geom_text(aes(x=col, y=row-0.20, label=examples), color="#52514E", size=3.1, lineheight=1.0) +
  geom_text(data=col_headers, aes(x=col, y=2.65, label=label),
            fontface="bold", size=4.3, color="#0B0B0B", inherit.aes=FALSE) +
  geom_text(data=row_headers, aes(x=0.52, y=row, label=label),
            hjust=1, size=3.6, color="#0B0B0B", lineheight=0.95, inherit.aes=FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("Non-Routine Cognitive"="#fc8d62", "Non-Routine Manual"="#e78ac3", "Routine Cognitive"="#66c2a5", "Routine Manual"="#8da0cb"), guide="none") +
  scale_linetype_identity() +
  scale_linewidth_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0.05, 2.55), ylim=c(0.5, 2.85), clip="off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin=margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
        plot.background=element_rect(fill=NA, color=NA),
        plot.title=element_text(face="bold", size=13, hjust=0.5)) +
  labs(title="The Four Task Groups")
```

We estimate a panel regression with year indicators and standard errors clustered by county, which recovers the association while accounting for the dependence among repeated observations of the same county. Diagnostics on that specification motivated a log respecification, and random forest and neural network models tested whether a more flexible form found signal the linear specification missed. Complexity increases only where the diagnostics show a simpler specification falling short, and @sec-analysis reports where each model landed.

Our primary finding is that a one percentage point shift toward non-routine manual work and away from non-routine cognitive work is associated with roughly \$846 less in purchasing power, with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus \$38, evaluated at the panel mean. Task groups can be measured for any county from public data, and where they are associated with purchasing power they point to economic strain that poverty and unemployment rates alone do not register.
